title: Counting Bits
description: DP on bits: counts[i] = counts[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — reuse the answer for half of i. O(n).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: given a non-negative integer `n`, return an array of length `n+1` where `result[i]` is the count of 1-bits in `i` (the popcount). A few quick checks:"

• Is `n` always >= 0, and what's the upper bound? (Bit DP allocates n+1 slots, so a huge n forces an O(n) memory trade.)
• Should the output be an array, or are we allowed to return any iterable / stream the answers?
• Index 0 — should the array START at 0 (so length n+1), or is the prompt 1-indexed?
• Can I assume integer arithmetic and standard JS bitwise semantics (signed int32)?
sections.why: The 'array of length n+1, indexed from 0' detail is what shapes the loop bound and the base case — getting it wrong is an off-by-one waiting to happen. Asking about the upper bound on n matters because the whole point of the bit-DP approach is to trade O(n) memory for O(n) time vs. naïve O(n log n); if n is enormous, you'd want to know whether the interviewer wants per-query popcount instead (in which case Brian Kernighan or a builtin is the better fit).

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n log n) solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is to popcount each `i` independently: for each `i` from 0 to n, walk its bits (either with `n & (n-1)` repeatedly, or by checking `i & (1 << k)` for k = 0..31) and tally. That's O(n log n) total — O(log i) per number, summed over n.

A second brute force is to call a builtin if one existed — but JS doesn't ship a popcount, so you'd write the bit-loop yourself."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the brute force out loud. (1) It establishes the baseline you're beating — going from O(n log n) to O(n) is a meaningful improvement, but only meaningful if the interviewer sees the starting point. (2) It seeds the DP insight: the brute force recomputes popcount independently for every i, which is wasteful because adjacent integers share most of their bits. That waste is exactly what the DP recurrence eliminates.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to bit-DP?
sections.say:
"The trigger: the answer for `i` can be expressed using the answer for a strictly smaller index — that's the DP shape. Specifically, `i >> 1` is `i` with the lowest bit dropped (integer divide by 2), and `i & 1` recovers that lowest bit. So `popcount(i) = popcount(i >> 1) + (i & 1)` — exactly one fewer bit on the right side of the recurrence, so the DP fills bottom-up in one pass.

"The structural property: every integer's bit pattern is its half's bit pattern with one extra bit on the end. Once you see that, the table fills itself — every entry references one earlier entry, and base case `counts[0] = 0` anchors it."
sections.why: Naming the bit identity `i = (i >> 1) << 1 | (i & 1)` is the move — it's the algebraic equality that justifies the DP recurrence. Without it you're just asserting that the recurrence works; with it you're proving it. The shape of the dependency (each `i` references `i >> 1`, which is strictly smaller) is what makes the bottom-up fill safe — there's no risk of reading an uninitialized cell because the half is always already computed. That's the same dependency-direction argument that justifies any 1D bottom-up DP.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me fill the table for a couple of inputs to make sure the recurrence is right." Three cases — the textbook small n, a degenerate n=0 base-only case, and a slightly larger n that crosses the next power of two so you see the pattern reset.

examples.note: Classic textbook trace — fills six cells.
Degenerate — the loop never runs, just the base case.
examples.trace:
counts = [0]
loop condition i<=0 with i=1 → false, never enters
return [0] ✓

examples.note: Sanity-check up to 7 = 0b111 — the all-ones value at the top of the third bit row.

sections.why: Two things the trace surfaces. (1) The off-by-one risk: the loop must start at `i=1`, not `i=0`, because `0 >> 1 = 0` would try to read `counts[0]` while writing it — fine numerically but a confusing self-reference. (2) The reset-at-power-of-two pattern: notice that `counts[4]` matches `counts[2]` which matches `counts[1]` — every power of two has exactly one bit, and the table re-uses that fact rather than recomputing. The third example shows the all-ones at the top of the byte-row, which is the case where popcount is at its local max.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• n=0 → return `[0]`. The loop simply doesn't fire because `1 <= 0` is false. ✓
• Very large n → memory becomes the binding constraint (n+1 array slots). For n in the billions, you'd switch to per-query popcount instead of building the table.
• n approaching 2^31 — at the upper edge of signed int32, `i >> 1` still works because the input `i` is the array INDEX, not a bit-pattern we're manipulating raw — JS array indices accept values up to 2^32 - 1. So no >>> coercion needed.
• Negative n — the loop bound `i <= n` would never enter for n<0, so you'd silently return an array of size `Math.max(0, n+1)`. I'd add a guard or ask the interviewer about the contract.
• Returning a typed array — for very large n, a `Uint8Array(n+1)` would be 4x smaller than a regular JS Array of small numbers. Worth flagging as a memory optimization.
sections.why: The 'very large n' edge is the structural one — it's the only case where the algorithm choice changes. Brian Kernighan's per-query popcount is O(log i) per query but O(1) space, while this DP is O(1) per query but O(n) space; the right choice depends on how many queries you'll make and how big n is. Mentioning the typed-array option signals you've thought about real-world memory layout, which is the kind of detail that wins points in a systems-leaning interview.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — exactly one pass from 1 to n, with O(1) work per iteration (one shift, one mask, one add, one array write).

Space is O(n) for the output array itself; auxiliary space is O(1).

If you wanted to extend this: an alternate DP uses `counts[i] = counts[i & (i-1)] + 1`, where `i & (i-1)` is `i` with its LOWEST set bit cleared (the Brian Kernighan move). Same O(n), same DP shape — just a different bit identity. The first form (`i >> 1 + i & 1`) splits off the LAST bit; this alternate splits off the LOWEST set bit. Both are valid; the right-shift version is more intuitive because it maps directly to integer division by 2."
sections.why: The amortized analysis here is trivial — there's no nested loop to defend. The structural payoff is the comparison to the alternate DP: presenting both recurrences shows you see this as a TEMPLATE (any bit identity that strips one bit produces a valid DP), not as a one-shot trick. That generalization is also what unlocks more exotic problems — for example, `counts[i] = counts[i ^ (i & -i)] + 1` uses yet another bit identity to strip the lowest set bit and works equally well.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the bit-DP table fill. Each row shows `i`, `i >> 1` (i with the lowest bit dropped), and `i & 1` (the lowest bit) — all in binary — so you can see the recurrence `counts[i] = counts[i>>1] + lowbit` literally adding one bit at a time.

yield { line: 3, label: `init counts of size ${n + 1} filled with 0`, state: { n, counts: [...counts] } };
yield { line: 4, label: `outer step: i=${i} (${bin(i)})`, state: { n, i: `${i} (${bin(i)})`, half: `${half} (${bin(half)})`, low, counts: [...counts] } };

notes: `i >> 1` is integer divide by 2 — drops the lowest bit, which (i & 1) recovers.
counts[0] = 0 is the base case; the loop starts at 1.
Naive popcount per i is O(log i) → O(n log n) total; this DP is O(n).

questions.q: What does `i >> 1` compute for non-negative i?
options: The bit-reverse of i within its current bit-width
The highest set bit of i (the position of the most significant 1)
The lowest bit of i (0 or 1)
The popcount of i mod 2 (the parity of bits)
Bits in i = bits in i/2 plus its last bit
Because `i >> 1` always equals `popcount(i) - 1`, so adding the parity recovers the full count
Because every integer i has exactly `floor(log2(i)) + 1` set bits, and the recurrence reconstructs that
Because `i & 1` doubles the bit count when set, matching the doubling effect of the left-shift inverse

exercises.prompt: Fill in the bit-DP popcount table.

L3.prompt: Write `countBits(n)` returning an array where `counts[i]` is the number of 1-bits in `i` for i = 0..n. Use the O(n) DP `counts[i] = counts[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`. Log `JSON.stringify(countBits(5))`.
hints: Allocate counts of size n+1; base case counts[0] = 0.
`i >> 1` is i/2 floored; `i & 1` is i mod 2.
